A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Volumetric Functional Maps and retain the same methodological and experimental backbone. All 13 pages of v1 and 19 pages of v3 are readable, including v3's Appendices A–I; v1 has no appendices. Figures, tables, and equations support reliable comparison.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original correspondence errors, runtimes, connectivity-transfer results, and brain-segmentation demonstrations, including experiments on 40 volumetric shape pairs and several surface-matching datasets.

after.justification: v3 retains original experiments and adds geodesic-distortion and boundary-reconstruction analyses, additional map-quality measurements, and an aggregate untangling evaluation.

M1.justification: The tetrahedral cotangent-Laplacian framework, functional coordinate transfer, spectral extrapolation, and volume-aware surface correspondence remain the same. CMH, Orthoprods, and ZoomOut already appear in v1. Newly stated boundary conditions and pseudocode document the existing procedures without establishing an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: Both versions use Su et al.'s volumetric shapes, SHREC’19, SHREC’20, TOPKIDS, and the same brain-segmentation setting. The Nigolian/Garanzha untangling-failure scenario already appears in v1 Figure 7; v3 expands its evaluated sample. New appendix diagnostics use existing shapes rather than introducing another population or application domain.

E2.justification: Surface-matching comparisons expand from one reported basis per dataset in v1 Table 2 to LBO, CMH, and Orthoprods comparisons on every retained dataset in v3 Table 2. These add comparator variants within the corresponding comparisons. The principal FMaps, ZoomOut, ZoomOut Fast, Orthoprods, and Garanzha untangling methods are retained.

E3.justification: Appendix B introduces Weyl-adjusted spectral comparisons and changes the Laplacian-commutativity normalization. New protocols include 100,000 random point pairs per shape pair for geodesic distortion, boundary reconstruction across basis sizes 50–500, and additional continuity, coverage, Dirichlet-energy, and flip metrics. Section 5.2 reports evaluation over 1,405 untangling failures, where v1 supplied an illustrative rescue.

E4.justification: v3 adds analyses of surface-versus-volume geodesic distortion, boundary traces' ability to reconstruct surface eigenfunctions, and broader basis-dependent matching failures. Untangling validation becomes substantially more systematic. The original flip-versus-basis-size curves are retained in Appendix F, so their relocation alone is not counted as new analysis.

E5.justification: Appendix C and Figure 11 newly report mean geodesic distortion with standard deviations over sampled point pairs. These describe variation within the sampled data, not repeated-run uncertainty. Neither version reports multi-seed performance estimates, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds many basis-specific results and revises existing entries: SHREC’19 LBO success changes from 100% to 53.15% despite unchanged reported AGEs, and SHREC’20 CMH success changes from 92.73% to 55.49%. New entries show surface methods outperforming volumetric LBO and Orthoprods on SHREC’20. v3 also reports rescuing 85% of 1,405 untangling failures and adds diagnostic results. Revised spectral histograms use changed normalization and therefore do not establish same-setting gains.

T1.justification: v1 infers a left inverse from the boundary matrix being tall; v3 adds a cited Neumann-boundary linear-independence argument. Appendix B introduces Weyl-law reasoning for transforming volumetric eigenvalues by a power of 3/2 and changes the commutativity denominator from ||C|| to ||CΛ_M||. These substantially extend mathematical justification and revise a formal metric definition without changing the mapping algorithm.

C1.justification: The abstracts, introductions, and conclusions retain the central claims: the first volumetric extension of functional maps, applications to signal and connectivity transfer, and improved surface correspondence. Both abstracts retain the claim of consistently outperforming surface-only spectral methods. Added validation does not redefine these core contributions.

C2.justification: v3 explains that VOL is relatively easy and benefits from volumetric information only with Orthoprods, and that SHREC’20 can favor surface methods unless CMH compensates for topological errors. Appendix F newly recommends LBO for small bases and CMH for larger ones; Appendix D qualifies boundary traces as useful but potentially suboptimal. These materially expand applicability qualifications beyond v1's predominantly favorable interpretation.

D1.justification: v3 supplies a code-access URL, pseudocode for all three procedures, explicit cotangent weights and Neumann conditions, and concrete basis settings. Examples include 20×20 maps expanded to 120×120 with ZoomOut steps of five and 500 eigenfunctions for untangling. These fill substantial documentation gaps in v1; they do not establish that previously reported experiments used different settings.

R1.justification: Targeted additions acknowledge LDDMM volumetric registration and Raviv et al.'s volumetric heat-kernel descriptors, and cite additional work on Laplacian discretization, spectral approximation, and boundary traces. These broaden contextual grounding while retaining the existing positioning relative to piece-wise mappings and surface functional maps.

P1.justification: The main text is extensively condensed and rewritten. The former spectral-validation subsection moves into Appendix B, while dataset discussion and basis analysis are reorganized into Appendices G–H, alongside new explanatory and algorithmic appendices. Terminology, headings, citation style, and author ordering also change.

P2.justification: The document is comprehensively reformatted. Table 2 becomes a full-width three-basis comparison, and the four matching plots expand into twelve panels in Figure 15. v3 adds an extrapolation diagram, distortion and reconstruction plots, a metrics table, and algorithm boxes; it also splits, relocates, resizes, and rearranges existing illustrations.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves reproducibility and scrutiny of the method by supplying implementation parameters and pseudocode, exposing basis-dependent failures through fuller comparisons, and testing assumptions about volumetric distortion and boundary representation. The aggregate untangling evaluation strengthens practical validation beyond v1's isolated example. Important weaknesses remain: revised success rates are unexplained, and the retained consistent-superiority claim conflicts with Table 2. Nevertheless, the increased transparency and targeted validation provide a substantial net quality gain.
